abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a groundbreaking theoretical framework that reconceptualizes parallel algorithm design through the lens of quantum-classical hybrid computation models. Unlike conventional parallel computing theories that assume deterministic task decomposition, our approach leverages probabilistic workload distribution informed by quantum entanglement principles to achieve unprecedented parallelization efficiency. We present rigorous mathematical foundations demonstrating that quantum-inspired task scheduling on heterogeneous many-core processors can overcome classical complexity barriers in load balancing problems. The theoretical analysis establishes novel bounds on parallel speedup that transcend Amdahl's law, proving that certain problem classes achieve super-linear speedup under quantum-classical scheduling. We introduce the concept of Entangled Parallelism Coefficient (EPC), which characterizes the maximum achievable parallelism in systems exhibiting quantum correlation patterns. Experimental validation on a hybrid quantum-classical testbed confirms theoretical predictions, showing 3.2x speedup over state-of-the-art heuristics for NP-hard graph partitioning problems. This work establishes a new paradigm in parallel algorithm theory, opening research directions that bridge quantum computing and traditional high-performance computing for next-generation architectures.

Performance modeling for GPU-accelerated systems remains challenged by inaccurate communication cost estimation in modern interconnect topologies. This paper presents an enhanced analytical model that significantly improves performance prediction accuracy for parallel applications on multi-GPU distributed environments. Our approach extends the LogGP model by incorporating adaptive bandwidth saturation factors and hierarchical contention modeling for modern network-on-chip architectures. The improved model introduces the Hierarchical Communication Overhead Function (HCOF) that captures non-uniform memory access patterns across heterogeneous compute nodes. Theoretical analysis derives closed-form expressions for optimal problem decomposition sizes that minimize total execution time under bandwidth constraints. Validation against fifteen HPC benchmarks demonstrates prediction error reduction from 18.7% (traditional LogGP) to 4.3% (proposed model) on average. We further provide analytical guidelines for optimal kernel fusion strategies that maximize effective memory bandwidth utilization. This work delivers practical analytical tools for parallel algorithm designers seeking to optimize communication patterns on contemporary GPU clusters.

We present Hermes, a novel hierarchical runtime system designed for exascale heterogeneous architectures that fundamentally reimagines fault tolerance in parallel computing. Unlike traditional checkpoint-restart approaches incurring 25-40% overhead, Hermes employs a proactive fault management paradigm integrating hardware-level anomaly detection with intelligent process migration. The system architecture introduces three key innovations: a lightweight distributed heartbeat mechanism achieving microsecond-scale fault detection latency, a prediction-driven pre-emptive migration scheduler using machine learning models trained on hardware failure traces, and a novel incremental checkpoint compression technique reducing checkpoint data volume by 85%. Hermes runtime automatically restructures application communication patterns to bypass failed nodes while maintaining global consistency through epoch-based synchronization. Evaluation on 10,000-core GPU clusters demonstrates fault recovery overhead below 3% compared to 28% for conventional coordinated checkpointing, while achieving 99.7% overall application completion rate under realistic failure scenarios. The system supports popular programming models including OpenMP, CUDA, and MPI through modular plug-in interfaces, enabling seamless integration with existing HPC software stacks.

Energy efficiency has become a critical constraint in modern parallel computing, yet existing power-aware scheduling strategies inadequately address the complex trade-offs in heterogeneous GPU clusters. This paper presents EcoSched, an improved energy-aware task scheduler that significantly advances state-of-the-art DVFS and power capping techniques for parallel workloads. EcoSched introduces a two-phase optimization approach: offline profiling generates workload-specific power-performance Pareto frontiers, while online scheduling dynamically adapts frequency/voltage settings based on real-time performance telemetry and deadline constraints. The system incorporates a novel Contention-Aware Power budgeting algorithm that distributes power headroom across nodes to maximize aggregate throughput under cluster-wide power limits. We implement EcoSched as a lightweight extension to existing resource managers including Slurm and PBS, requiring no application code modifications. Extensive evaluation across 12 scientific applications on NVIDIA DGX-2 clusters demonstrates 31% energy reduction with less than 5% performance degradation, achieving 2.1x improvement in energy-delay product compared to prior power-aware schedulers. The system gracefully handles interference from co-located workloads while maintaining quality of service for latency-sensitive applications.
